newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh chambers decry poor business climate.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh chambers decry poor business climate.

text.p: Bangladesh's business chambers said on Tuesday they were worried about the business climate in the country and concerned economic growth targets might not be met.
"The country's macro-economic fundamentals are under pressure. This has already threatened the investment climate, upset trade and industry," six leading trade bodies said in a joint statement.
"If the trend continues it will be impossible to achieve this year's (1997/98 July-June) envisaged growth rate (of six percent)," the statement warned.
"We urge the government to immediately review the reasons for a liquidity crisis in the banks," the statement said.

Bank officials said the liquidity shortage was caused by heavy defaults in loans totalling 150 billion taka -- 90 percent of them from state-owned banks. Some 35 billion taka had been recovered since the government launched a special drive early this year.
The business groups also expressed concern over a drop in foreign exchange reserves, which stood at $1.62 billion in July, down from $1.99 in July 1996.
The current reserves were equivalent to three months imports, bank officials said.

"These problems, coupled with energy scarcity and unbelievable harassment of business people of all categories by local mastans (hooligans) make it increasingly difficult to pursue normal business and industrial activities," the statement said.

"Tight monetary policy, liquidity problems in the banks arising from large-scale borrowing by the government and the state-owned enterprises, reluctance on the part of the banks to take initiatives (to punish offenders)...have brought about near stalemate in financing new investment."
The government plans to launch a 10 billion taka industrial bonds for long-term financing of industrial projects in the private sector.
The trade bodies also said the government had failed to take measures "to save the collapsing stock market".

The Dhaka Stock Exchange all-share price index dropped to 867.79 on Tuesday. The DSE index climbed to 3,600 during October-November last year, but started dipping early this year after alleged price manipulation.
"Shortage of energy remains a serious problem," said the statement, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.
The business bodies also criticised poor management and frequent unrest in the country's main Chittagong port.
"This is most unfortunate. We repeatedly stressed that Chittagong Port must function efficiently, free from political interferences and unruly trade union elements."
